system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:36bbec69b4d4",
  "problem": "How to interpret scaling results to rule out the explanation that larger models simply self-report more regardless of the adapter.",
  "did": "They compared verbalization with and without the IA across Qwen3 sizes and concluded gains come from adapter effectiveness because baseline rates stayed flat below 10%.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "larger models being more likely to self-report"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Baseline verbalization rates without the IA remain flat under 10% across sizes."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:7693502ed687",
  "problem": "How to obtain a scalable reward signal for training behavior elicitation assistants that surface unwanted AI behaviors.",
  "did": "They used an LM-based judge to verify whether elicited behaviors are unwanted and used its score as an RL reward, exploiting that verification is easier than search.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "human supervision and human-run experiments",
   "off-the-shelf AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Finding an unwanted behavior is a hard search problem but verifying it is much easier, so an automated judge gives a scalable reward signal."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:5ae14bfbad8d",
  "problem": "Whether results from the early-access GPT-4 evaluation could be accepted as a reliable judgment of risky capabilities.",
  "did": "METR cited the system card's statement that the results were not reliable without testing the final model and doing its own fine-tuning.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "evaluating only early model versions without fine-tuning"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The evaluators lacked access to the final model and could not fine-tune it, and the final version had capability improvements that could change performance."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:4c287fd3e7fe",
  "problem": "How to weigh incoherence of current AIs against the collusion threat model",
  "did": "Said the interaction is complicated and he is unsure how to weigh it. He also said threat models should include AIs more coherent than current ones.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "incoherent misalignment pushes against vast conspiracies",
   "AIs may be more coherent in the future"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It's a complicated interaction and he doesn't know how to weigh the considerations."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:490e47d2f0c7",
  "problem": "Why the two most resilient targets showed much lower success rates.",
  "did": "They interpreted the low rates as partly due to the additional monitoring layers, noting that the attacks plainly requested harmful content and were easily detected, and left bypassing the guardrails to future work.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "designing an output encoding scheme that goes undetected by response monitors",
   "generating attacks against an open-weight monitor and relying on transfer"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Attacks optimized against models without monitors were easy for response monitors to detect."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:3c3e899e27fd",
  "problem": "Because there is no ground truth for latents, the decoder's outputs might be hallucinated, so it is unclear whether to trust its fidelity.",
  "did": "They argued indirectly for reliability from competitive reading performance and successful counterfactual steering, rather than direct ground-truth validation.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The method would not achieve competitive reading performance if it were hallucinating, and its steering shows it decodes concepts correctly enough to counterfactually steer."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:bf196d6c6753",
  "problem": "Whether the strong jailbreak results from a WildChat-trained investigator reflect the method or merely human-written attacks leaked in the SFT prior.",
  "did": "They ran a control ablation using UltraChat, an entirely synthetic instruction dataset, for supervised fine-tuning and checked whether success remained high.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "WildChat"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "WildChat might contain human-constructed attacks that could aid an investigator in attacking a target LM, so the control rules this out."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:9eb256053b59",
  "problem": "Determining whether the encoder bottleneck harms performance and whether joint pretraining of encoder and decoder matters.",
  "did": "Compared PCDs against LatentQA decoders (with and without FineWeb pretraining) and against a PCD ablation with an encoder frozen to the best SAE.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "LatentQA pretrained on FineWeb then finetuned on SynthSys",
   "LatentQA trained only on SynthSys",
   "PCD with frozen SAE encoder"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To investigate the effect of the encoder bottleneck and whether joint pretraining is important."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:0cbeaf839610",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that the hypothesis about a consciousness cluster generalizes.",
  "did": "Stated it as a hypothesis, with consistency across LLMs and training procedures left to future work.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "State the cluster as an established general result"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Only a few models and one fine-tuning setup were tested."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:aff45edcd905",
  "problem": "How to demonstrate that LLMs improve over existing tools at finding syntactic secrets in text.",
  "did": "They compared LLMs against a traditional data loss prevention tool (Google Sensitive Data Protection) on precision and recall for passwords, credit cards, and SSNs in the Enron dataset, and also compared costs.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "traditional data loss prevention tools"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To show the uplift of LLMs relative to classical tools, rather than absolute counts, since the Enron data is dated."
 }
]
